title: The double sigh
hookLine: two inhales, one long exhale; a small 2023 Stanford study found daily sighing lifted mood (Balban et al.)

cards: Watch a small child who has cried for a long time and is finally calming down. Listen to the breathing. There's a catch in it: a little in-breath, another little in-breath on top of it, then a long, shaky breath out.
A hiccup and a sigh at once. Adults do it too, without noticing, in sleep and on the edge of tears. It works like one of the body's own reset buttons, and nobody has to install it.
Today, press it on purpose: the double sigh.

teach.b: Breathing researchers call it the physiological sigh. Two inhales through the nose, the second a short top-up on the first, then one long exhale through the mouth.
People sigh like this on their own every few minutes, and more often when they're stressed.
One idea about why: deep in the lungs are millions of tiny air sacs, and some slowly go flat when breathing is shallow.
The second inhale helps pop them open again, and the long exhale lets the body let go of more carbon dioxide.
In 2023 a team at Stanford, led by Melis Balban with David Spiegel and Andrew Huberman, tried something simple. About a hundred people did five minutes of breathing a day for a month.
Some did slow sighs like this, some did other breathing patterns, and some did a short mindfulness meditation. Everyone's mood improved a bit.
The sighing group improved the most, and their breathing rate at rest came down.

teach.h: ONE SMALL STUDY. HOLD IT LIGHTLY.
teach.b: That's worth knowing, and worth holding lightly: it was one small study, done remotely, at home, and it needs repeating before anyone builds a big claim on it. What it adds is permission.
A sigh isn't only something that happens to you when you're sad or tired. You can do it on purpose, gently, to tell the body the moment has passed. Sighing on purpose is not rudeness.

how: The physiological sigh, two inhales through the nose and a long exhale through the mouth, happens on its own every few minutes; since the 2023 Stanford study, some people also use it on purpose for a minute or a few minutes a day.

games.q: Stanford researchers ask about a hundred people to breathe five minutes a day for a month, in different ways. which group's mood lifts the most?
o: the ones doing slow double sighs.
games.why: everyone improved a bit, and the sighing group improved the most. a small study, but a surprising one: the humblest breath came out on top.

practice: Sit or stand with loose shoulders, breathe in through your nose fairly full, then, without letting any out, sip in a little more on top, and let it all go slowly through your mouth.
Do three of these sighs with a few ordinary breaths between them, soft, not a workout. In between, let the breath be whatever it is, and notice what your shoulders and jaw do.

wordCard.voice: Suspirium. Latin for a sigh: two inhales and one long exhale, the body's own reset, done on purpose. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a sigh, a deep breath. The root spirare, to breathe, is also in spirit and inspire.

carryVoice: Your line: sigh on purpose. The humblest breath came out on top. See you tomorrow.
